A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same four-variant reward-model study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model training and evaluation on mathematical benchmarks and MMLU-Pro, together with noise, reasoning-length, and single-domain training analyses.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, and LEXam evaluations, additional model and training controls, and filtering experiments.

M1.justification: The four core formulations, losses, and default inference procedures remain unchanged. v3 adds tested procedural variants involving Gemini-refined process labels, relaxed gPRM consensus filtering, and alternative dPRM aggregation rules (Appendix G). These are limited adaptations within the existing framework.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on graduate-level science questions in GPQA-Diamond and specialized medical and legal examination questions in MedQA and LEXam. Testing MMLU-Pro-trained verifiers on these datasets substantially expands coverage beyond the retained mathematical benchmarks and MMLU-Pro evaluation.

E2.justification: The four verifier variants and majority voting remain the principal comparisons. Tables 7–12 additionally compare label-refined or relaxed-filtering PRMs and product, mean, and last-step dPRM aggregation against the existing methods. Pass@N is added as an oracle reference.

E3.justification: v3 adds cross-dataset transfer evaluation with N=16, restricts MedQA/LEXam comparisons to two generators, introduces a Qwen3-8B verifier backbone, and evaluates additional learning rates, LoRA ranks, and aggregation settings. Some Appendix F backbone identifications and the length-bin boundaries in v1 Figure 38/v3 Figure 9b also change; these reported revisions do not establish that the corresponding experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether PRM weaknesses depend on distilled backbones, hyperparameter choices, aggregation rules, label quality, or strict consensus filtering (Figure 37 and Tables 3, 5–12). v1 Figure 39's per-dataset 'aha' breakdown is removed. The complete label-noise study moves from v1 Figure 40 to v3 Figure 11 and is not a new analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix D changes the reported replication from three independent runs for mathematics and one for multi-domain experiments to five independent runs, except experiments using R1-Distill-Llama-8B or Qwen3-8B. v3 also lists checkpoints for seeds 1–5. This is an explicit expansion of reported replication.

E6.justification: v3 adds specialized-benchmark, backbone, tuning, filtering, aggregation, and timing results, and revises several retained curves. Newly reported Table 7 gives N=16 gPRM accuracy of 64.26%, 64.84% with label refinement, and 64.82% with relaxed filtering, versus 70.02% for gORM. These are additional comparisons within v3, not version-to-version performance gains. The per-dataset 'aha' results in v1 Figure 39 disappear.

T1.justification: Appendix A replaces per-step variance floors with average variance floors and replaces the aggregate anti-correlation assumption with finite-window dependence bounded by rho. The resulting bounds use 2k rho instead of 2 gamma, with revised derivations. The mean-gPRM proof also removes unexplained sigma_A-squared and gamma_A terms present in v1. The overall length-growth conclusion remains.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a controlled four-variant evaluation across 14 domains, comparable multi-domain performance of dORM and dPRM, gORM's overall robustness, and length/noise explanations for PRM weaknesses. The added benchmarks and controls principally supply further evidence for these retained claims.

C2.justification: v3 clarifies that outcome supervision still allows ORMs to use intermediate reasoning, adds an annotation-reliability qualification to the 'aha' analysis, and interprets refinement and relaxed filtering as insufficient to resolve gPRM's weakness. It also removes v1's explicit limitation that verifiable-outcome results may not generalize to open-ended generation.

D1.justification: v3 adds seed-specific and Qwen3-8B checkpoint listings, access entries for the new evaluation datasets, blank-category prompt instructions, label-refinement details, and inference timings. Existing prompts and most training hyperparameters remain. The explicit 750/650-token sequence-limit statement in v1 is removed, without establishing an actual change to those limits.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for GPQA, MedQA, LEXam, Gemini, and She et al.'s R-PRM. It also expands discussion of the already-cited Uesato et al. work to acknowledge strong outcome-supervision results while distinguishing policy training from test-time verification. The broader research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and Appendix A–G organization are retained. v3 edits the abstract, introduction, and method explanations, presents informal theorem summaries in the main text, expands the practical-guidance discussion, and removes Appendix H's LLM-use disclosure. These refine the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the displays and adopts a different publication layout. Figure 6 combines multiple benchmarks, existing 'aha' and shuffled-reasoning plots are merged, length analyses are combined, and detailed MMLU-Pro plots move to Appendix F. New and expanded tables present tuning, filtering, and aggregation comparisons.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the recommendations through cross-dataset evaluations, reported five-run replication, and controls addressing backbone, tuning, aggregation, and filtering explanations. These address v1's reliance on one multi-domain benchmark and single-run multi-domain results. Appendix A also improves proof consistency. Removing the detailed 'aha' breakdown and open-ended-generation limitation reduces transparency, but the stronger validation provides a substantial net improvement.
